source.title: Universal Sparse Autoencoders: Interpretable Cross-Model Concept Alignment
source.authors: Harrish Thasarathan; J. Forsyth; Thomas Fel; Matthew Kowal; K. Derpanis

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The abstract begins with a truncated word, but the rest of the paper is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares concepts learned by universal and independently trained SAEs. The reported overlap is limited and varies by model, and the authors say universal training also discovers representations not found by model-specific training. This refines the claim that SAE features are canonical units.
record.gate_note: The paper studies vision models, not toy superposition networks or LLMs. Its relevant result is the measured overlap between USAE concepts and independently trained SAE concepts (Fig. 7 and Fig. 16); no results test feature sparsity, importance-dependent geometry, or one-dimensional directions.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces a method, Universal SAEs, that uses SAEs as a tool on three vision models. Its overlap analysis (Fig. 7, Fig. 16) compares the authors' own USAE dictionary with standard single-model SAEs to validate the method. The authors frame it as their method beating a random baseline. The USAE is trained on a different objective (cross-model reconstruction), and the authors say outright that this selects for shared concepts. So low overlap does not show that standard SAE features are non-canonical, unstable or incomplete. The study runs no seed-to-seed or size-to-size stability test, no completeness test and no canonicality test of ordinary SAEs. It does not touch toy-model geometry, the causes of polysemanticity, LLMs or feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that universal training recovers a significant fraction of the concepts learned by independent single-model SAEs, especially the highly co-firing ones. They also conclude that it uncovers shared representations that do not appear in model-specific training. Their framing is a validation of USAEs as an interpretability tool, not a test of whether SAE features are canonical.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a shared sparse autoencoder across multiple pretrained vision models and compares its concepts with independently trained SAEs; it does not reproduce the original toy-model setup or method.
record.method_sensitivity: Concept overlap differs by model and is higher when analysis is restricted to the top 1,000 co-firing concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: For each model, only 23–38% of concepts in a dictionary trained on a joint cross-model objective match the same-size single-model SAE dictionary (cosine similarity above 0.5). The match rate is higher for the top co-firing concepts (AUC 0.40–0.65, against a random baseline of 0.13).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The features a sparse dictionary recovers depend on the training objective; dictionaries trained with different objectives on the same activations share only part of their features.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The reported overlap is a cosine-similarity comparison between different SAE training regimes, not a test of completeness or stability across repeated runs. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for these overlap values.
record.rows_left_out: No other result rows were included: the other reported reconstruction, co-firing, firing-entropy, and activation-maximization results do not directly measure whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units.

untested.parts: Toy-model geometry, the sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry: not studied.
Capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity: not studied.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure: not studied.
No LLMs studied. SAEs are applied to vision models only, as a tool.
No test of completeness, of stability across seeds or sizes, or of canonicality for standard SAEs. The only comparison is USAE vs SAE, which differ in training objective.
The dimensionality of features is not studied.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper on vision models (SigLIP, DinoV2, ViT). The reader's T5 'tests' call treated a check of the study's own method against standard SAEs as a test of V5; I reclassified it as T4. In the limitations section the authors speculate that uninterpretable concepts may still be in superposition, but they offer no evidence. The Fig. 16 numbers are AUCs, which the appendix text also describes as average cosine similarity.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or important features receiving dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
The paper studies vision models, not LLMs, and does not measure feature spread across neurons in LLMs.

The paper measures concept overlap across universal and independently trained SAEs, but does not establish completeness, stability across repeated training runs, or canonicality of the full model representation.
Whether the features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: SigLIP
rows.operation_detail: Compared USAE decoder concepts with concepts from an independently trained SAE using cosine similarity and Hungarian alignment.
rows.measure: Fraction of concepts with a cosine-similarity match above threshold
rows.note: The paper reports this as a relatively low proportion of overlap.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method (USAE) with an independent SAE, not standard SAEs across runs, so it can't test canonicality. The 23% is the fraction of concepts with cosine similarity above 0.5 (Fig. 7 right); the random baseline is 0.00, and the AUC is 0.30.

rows.subject: DinoV2
rows.operation_detail: Compared USAE decoder concepts with concepts from an independently trained SAE using cosine similarity and Hungarian alignment.
rows.measure: Fraction of concepts with a cosine-similarity match above threshold
rows.note: The paper reports this as a relatively low proportion of overlap.
rows.check: Same issue as r1: own method vs independent SAE. The 26% is the fraction above 0.5; baseline 0.00, AUC 0.36.

rows.subject: ViT
rows.operation_detail: Compared USAE decoder concepts with concepts from an independently trained SAE using cosine similarity and Hungarian alignment.
rows.measure: Fraction of concepts with a cosine-similarity match above threshold
rows.note: This was the strongest overlap among the three models, but most concepts did not meet the reported threshold.
rows.check: Same issue as r1. The 38% is the fraction above 0.5; baseline 0.00, AUC 0.41. The caption's summary range of 23–37% is inconsistent with the 38% figure.

rows.subject: SigLIP
rows.operation_detail: Compared USAE concepts with independently trained SAE concepts, restricted to the top 1,000 co-firing concepts.
rows.note: Overlap is higher for this selected subset than in the broader comparison, but the authors still report model-to-model differences.
rows.check: The concept subset is a selection (top 1,000 co-firing concepts), and the comparison is still own method vs independent SAE. The 0.40 is labelled AUC in Fig. 16, though the appendix text calls it average cosine similarity. Random-baseline AUC is 0.13.

rows.subject: DinoV2
rows.operation_detail: Compared USAE concepts with independently trained SAE concepts, restricted to the top 1,000 co-firing concepts.
rows.note: This was the highest reported similarity in the selected subset.
rows.check: Same issue as r4. Value 0.65 (AUC per Fig. 16; random baseline 0.13).

rows.subject: ViT
rows.operation_detail: Compared USAE concepts with independently trained SAE concepts, restricted to the top 1,000 co-firing concepts.
rows.note: The selected concepts show greater alignment than the broad comparison, but the reported similarity is not complete.
rows.check: Same issue as r4. Value 0.52 (AUC per Fig. 16; random baseline 0.13).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Broad USAE-to-independent-SAE comparisons for SigLIP, DinoV2, and ViT
reader_labels.reason: Only 23%, 26%, and 38% of concepts, respectively, exceed cosine similarity 0.5, so the dictionaries do not align as complete canonical sets in these comparisons (r1–r3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Similarity is higher in this selected subset and varies across models (0.40, 0.65, and 0.52), showing that alignment depends on concept selection and model (r4–r6).
